open_obligations: Check that a stochastic oracle with constant advantage over random guessing is an adequate model of human error.
Note the authors themselves leave open oracles that give incorrect answers on some subset of queries.
Check whether the protocol requires the honest prover to run in polynomial time while the dishonest prover is unbounded; the cited passages do not state this.
If the honest prover must be efficient, check whether this requirement changes the class of decidable problems relative to PSPACE.
in.other_title: Theorem 6.2: stochastic-oracle doubly-efficient debate with cross-examination
in.rationale: Irving et al. note their theory models judges as error-free and agents as unbounded and call for richer models. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 6.2 gives a debate protocol with cross-examination for any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle Turing machine, with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5, in which the verifier V samples from the oracle O to check A's proposed distribution. The authors say human judgement is fallible and reward models approximate it from limited samples, so in practical settings the verifier's oracle O is likely to be flawed, and that Theorem 6.2 partially addresses this by making each response of O stochastic and allowing verification of any computation that outputs the correct answer with a constant advantage over random guessing. The cited passages do not say how the provers' running time is bounded, so the link does not cover Irving et al.'s unbounded agents.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate theory can drop the error-free judge of the DEBATE = PSPACE analogy, for K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machines whose stochastic oracle the verifier samples

open_obligations: Check that the expertise gap (hidden passage) is a fair stand-in for the capability gap Irving et al. target.
Check whether the debaters were trained toward equilibrium; if not, the result is about judge usability, not equilibrium behaviour.
Check whether the paper reports an upper bound on judge accuracy, and how it was computed, before reading the 84% as near-ceiling.
in.other_title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert judges: 84% vs 74% on hard reading comprehension questions
in.rationale: Irving et al. state debate had only an MNIST demonstration and that significant research is needed to know whether it works with human judges. Michael et al. report human-debater debates judged by non-expert humans reach 84% accuracy versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage; the paper also compares human with AI debaters.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate works in practice with human judges in natural language, on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage

text: The authors state that debate is at this point a proposal only for the natural-language case, that only a basic MNIST experiment has been demonstrated, and that significant research is required to know whether debate works in practice with human judges. They note that their DEBATE = PSPACE discussion models judges as limited but free of error and agents as having unlimited computational power, and call for richer theoretical models.
title: Debate is a proposal only for natural language; theory assumes error-free judges
